transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herfst.
The annual U.N. climate talks ended in a dramatic fashion without an agreement.
NPR's Julia Simon reports some are calling it the worst climate conference ever.
It's the longest climate conference in history, yet the conference ended without a deal.
The conference works by consensus, and countries disagreed about whether or not the text should mention transitioning away from fossil fuels.
Burning fossil fuels drives about 73 percent of planet heating emissions.
Yet some countries, like Saudi Arabia, opposed fossil fuel language.
Frustrated with the United Nations conference, more than 50 countries have started their own conference.
It's focused on transitioning away from oil, gas, and coal, and will have its second convening in July.
Meanwhile, countries are already moving away from oil and gas to solar and electric vehicles.
Not always for climate reasons, but economic ones.
Julia Simon, NPR News.
The Justice Department told a court the U.S. Army will detonate close to five tons of bomb-making material containing lead at a site in Iowa by Tuesday,
despite a court order pausing the detonation.
NPR's Andrea Hsu has more.
At issue are 68 drums of what the U.S. Army says is significantly degraded and unstable lead azide at a facility in Middletown, Iowa.
The Army has argued that because the material is at risk of exploding simultaneously, a planned explosion would be safer.
It had planned to detonate the material on Friday, a week after the EPA granted the Army an emergency permit,
but two environmental groups sued to block that permit, citing irreparable health and environmental harm and failure by the EPA to properly evaluate alternatives.
Last week, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily suspended the permit.
Now the Justice Department is arguing the Army does not need a permit and says it intends to act on Tuesday.
Andrea Hsu, NPR News.
It's a short trading week on Wall Street, with investors watching holiday shopping and home sales for clues about consumer spending.
NPR's Stephen Bassaha reports the Thanksgiving break follows a rough November for tech stocks.
Markets will be closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving, and tech companies might just be thankful for one less trading day.
The tech-heavy NASDAQ has been consistently trending down in November.
The S&P 500, Dow and the NASDAQ are now all in correction territory, meaning they are down more than 10 percent from a recent high.
Wednesday, the U.S. Census Bureau will release sales data for new homes in October.
Existing home sales that month were down almost 9 percent from a year earlier.
And Thanksgiving weekend, an estimated 183 million shoppers will be hunting for holiday deals,
according to the National Retail Federation, about 2 percent lower than last year.
Stephen Bassaha, NPR News.
U.S. futures contracts are trading higher at this hour.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
In Indonesia, three people are dead, dozens unaccounted for, in a fire at a canton factory in Bantan province.
Officials say 300 workers were inside when the fire broke out yesterday.
The cause remains unknown, but survivors say it started in a cooling unit.
Firefighters are still working to prevent re-ignition.
The death of a beloved hippo, Fiona, after she swallowed a knit hat,
has renewed calls to remind zoo visitors that animals can die from swallowing foreign objects.
And Fira Shondelis Duster has more.
While deaths like Fiona the hippos are rare, items such as coins, shoes and sunglasses frequently fall
and sometimes are tossed into animal habitats at zoos.
Dr. Gabrielle Aflaca, a veterinarian at Zoo Miami,
asks that visitors follow zoo etiquette and not yell or throw objects at the animals.
If we can just keep in mind that anything that we bring that could inadvertently end up in the animal exhibit
or somehow around the animal, try to just be mindful and not have your sunglasses on your head
if you're leaning over and looking at something.
Veterinarians say people should also be mindful of items that can harm animals in the wild or even pets at home.
Human medication should be stored properly and trash should be thrown into a garbage can so animals cannot eat it.
Shondelis Duster, NPR News.
The tech issue at Delta Airlines that delayed hundreds of flights today in and out of its busiest hub,
Atlanta's Hartsfield Jackson Airport, and around the country, is now fixed.
I'm Janine Herbst, NPR News, in Washington.
For more information on dining and entertainment, Capital One.
What's in your wallet? Terms apply. Details at CapitalOne.com.

topics.text: U.N. climate talks end without agreement after fossil fuel language dispute; 50+ countries start separate conference
Justice Department says Army will detonate 68 drums of lead azide in Middletown, Iowa, despite court pause
Wall Street trades short holiday week as tech-heavy NASDAQ, S&P 500 and Dow enter correction territory
Indonesia canton factory fire kills three, dozens unaccounted for in Bantan province
Death of hippo Fiona after swallowing knit hat renews warnings about zoo visitors feeding objects
Delta Airlines tech issue delaying hundreds of flights at Atlanta hub is now fixed
